title: North America capitals four of five · The Bahamas and the Leeward Islands
edition: North America capitals · Five regional lessons · John · November 2026
intro: Welcome to the North America capitals, episode four of five. First, I clear the chosen names for a fresh regional lesson.
Five capitals of the smaller islands: the Bahamas, then the Leeward chain of Saint Kitts, Antigua, Dominica and Saint Lucia.

states.name: Nassau
lines: Nassau stands on the harbour of New Providence, the small island where most of the Bahamas' people live.
Named in 1695 for William III, of the house of Orange-Nassau, it was a pirates' republic early in the eighteenth century, and Blackbeard lived here.
Remember Nassau as the pirates' republic of New Providence, named for William of Orange.

states.name: Basseterre
lines: Basseterre stands on the Caribbean side of Saint Kitts, in a lowland ringed by the island's volcanic hills.

French for "low land", and founded by the French in 1627; it is one of the oldest towns of the eastern Caribbean. Its Circus, a small roundabout with a clock, was modelled on Piccadilly Circus in London.
Remember Basseterre as the low land, with a roundabout copied from Piccadilly.

states.name: Saint John's
lines: Saint John's stands on the harbour of Antigua, the island Columbus named for a church in Seville.
The twin towers of its cathedral, rebuilt in stone after an earthquake in 1843, stand above the harbour, and Nelson's Dockyard, on the other side of the island, is a UNESCO site.
Remember Saint John's as the harbour above Nelson's Dockyard, with a cathedral rebuilt in stone after the earthquake of 1843.
states.transition: Let's bring Saint John's into view.

states.name: Roseau
lines: Roseau lies at the mouth of the Roseau river on the west coast of Dominica, below the mountains behind it.
French for "reed", for the reeds along its river; the Boiling Lake, a flooded fumarole, lies in the mountains behind the town.
Remember Roseau as the town of reeds, below the mountains and the Boiling Lake.

states.name: Castries
lines: Castries stands on a harbour on the west coast of Saint Lucia, with the hills of the island rising behind it.

Named for a French minister of the navy, the Marquis de Castries, it was burned several times and a blaze in 1948 took its old wooden centre. The poet Derek Walcott, a Nobel laureate, was born here in 1930.
Remember Castries as the harbour named for a French minister, and the birthplace of the Nobel poet Derek Walcott.

recap: Nassau stands alone on New Providence in the north, and the four island capitals step south along the Leewards: Basseterre, Saint John's, Roseau and Castries.
Remember the pirates' republic, the low land with its Piccadilly roundabout, the harbour above Nelson's Dockyard, the town of reeds and the harbour of the Nobel poet.
